notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Psalm 98, drawn from the sources I could access:

---

## Overview & Structure

The psalm is widely seen as having three stanzas of three verses each. Spurgeon and others identify the structure as: (a) vv. 1–3, the subject or grounds of praise; (b) vv. 4–6, the manner of praise; (c) vv. 7–9, the universal extent of praise. [https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps098.php]

This is the only psalm in the Psalter with the bare inscription “a psalm” (*mizmor*), with no other epithet. The Targum calls it “a psalm of prophecy,” and Jewish commentators (Jarchi, Aben Ezra, Abendana) connect it to the days of the Messiah. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-98.html]

---

## Verse 1

> *Sing to the LORD a new song, for He has done wonders; His right hand and holy arm have gained Him the victory.*

**The “new song.”** Commentators across traditions agree that a “new song” signals fresh, extraordinary praise — not merely repeating old forms. Spurgeon says the new song in Psalm 96 was because the Lord was coming; here it is because “he has come, and seen and conquered.” Calvin likewise says the expression denotes “an extraordinary, not a common, ascription of praise.” The Pulpit Commentary adds that the faithful steward “is ever bringing out of his treasures things which are at once old and new.” [https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps098.php; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-98.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-98.html]

**Marvellous things.** Gill sees these as Christ’s incarnation, miracles, redemption, resurrection, ascension, the gift of the Spirit, and the success of the Gospel among the Gentiles — all requiring a new song. Guzik adds that the worship must flow from “life experience of His marvelous things,” not empty singing. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-98.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-98/]

**“His right hand and His holy arm.”** The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Hebrew underlying “gotten him the victory” (KJV) is better rendered “hath wrought salvation for him” (RV), echoing Isaiah 59:16 and 63:5. Spurgeon sees these as the instruments of God’s unaided victory: “Sin, death, and hell fell beneath his solitary prowess.” The “holy arm” signals that the victory was won in a way consistent with divine holiness and justice. Gill: “His holy arm did it in a way that maintains and secures the glory of divine holiness and justice.” Guzik says the image of the “holy arm” is God rolling up His sleeve. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-98.html; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps098.php; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-98.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-98/]

**Tradition note — Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin stresses that “his own arm brought salvation” (Isa 59:16) means God saves “not by human means, or in an ordinary way, but delivering his Church in an unprecedented manner.” The arm of God “stands opposed to ordinary means.” This marks God’s sovereign initiative — salvation is entirely His work. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-98.html]

---

## Verse 2

> *The LORD has proclaimed His salvation and revealed His righteousness to the nations.*

**“Made known” / “openly shewed.”** The salvation God has wrought is not hidden — it is published before the nations. Spurgeon connects this to the outpouring of the Holy Spirit and the preaching of the Gospel to the Gentiles: “The Lord is to be praised not only for effecting human salvation, but also for making it known, for man would never have discovered it for himself.” The Pulpit Commentary adds: “God has vindicated in the eyes of all the nations upon earth the righteousness of his rule over mankind.” [https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps098.php; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-98.html]

**Salvation and righteousness as a pair.** Guzik, citing VanGemeren, notes that in Isaiah these two words are synonyms for the establishment of God’s just order. Gill explains “righteousness” here as Christ’s own righteousness, by which He fulfilled the law in the place of His people — now revealed openly in the Gospel, not in dark shadows. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-98/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-98.html]

Ellicott observes that the psalm “plainly belongs to that cycle of literature produced by the joy of the Restoration” and “is in fact little more than a compilation from Isaiah 40, 26, and from other psalms, especially Psalms 96.” [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/98.htm]

---

## Verse 3

> *He has remembered His love and faithfulness to the house of Israel; all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.*

**“Remembered.”** Calvin explains that “remembered” is language accommodated to human understanding — what has long been suspended seems forgotten. Over two thousand years elapsed from the promise to Abraham to Christ’s appearing. God’s remembering is motivated solely by His “mere good pleasure” and faithfulness to His promise, not by human merit. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-98.html]

**Love (mercy) and faithfulness (truth).** The Pulpit Commentary: “The judgment of the nations involves mercy and deliverance to Israel, which is oppressed by them; and thus manifests God’s faithfulness towards them.” The Expositor’s Bible Commentary adds that Israel appears here “rather as the recipient than as the celebrator of God’s lovingkindness.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-98.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-98.html]

**“All the ends of the earth.”** The universal scope is insisted upon. Guzik: “God’s work was centered in the house of Israel, but the ends of the earth were never to be forgotten. From the very beginning of His covenant plan with Abraham, all the families of the earth were in view (Genesis 12:3).” Calvin likewise: “The nations formerly immersed in delusions and superstitions would participate in it.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-98/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-98.html]

**Tradition note — Methodist/Wesleyan (Seedbed):** Brian Russell at Seedbed stresses that “there is always a missional dimension to the Lord’s actions. Salvation is never merely about us. Good news comes to us on its way to others.” The Lord’s actions for Israel “are ultimately actions for the world (Genesis 12:3b; Exodus 19:5–6; Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6).” [https://seedbed.com/gods-reign-brings-joy-to-the-world/]

---

## Verse 4

> *Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth; break forth — let your cry ring out, and sing praises!*

**Loud, enthusiastic praise.** The Hebrew verbs pile up (“make a joyful noise … break forth … cry ring out … sing praises”) to express intensity. The Pulpit Commentary: “God is to be praised heartily — with a loud and ringing voice. The body is to unite with the soul in giving him thanks, and to perform its part vigorously and with zeal.” Gill calls it “a heap of words … to express the intenseness of mind, vehemency of affection, and strength of spirit.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-98.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-98.html]

Spurgeon quotes John Wesley: “Sing lustily, and with a good courage. Beware of singing as if you were half dead or half asleep; but lift up your voice with strength. Be no more afraid of your voice now, nor more ashamed of its being heard, than when you sung the songs of Satan.” Guzik, citing Boice and Marvin Tate, notes that “the noise of temple worship was legendary” — in Ezra 3:13 the sound was “heard far away.” [https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps098.php; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-98/]

**“All the earth.”** The call has now expanded beyond Israel to embrace all nations. Calvin: “When God should break down the middle wall of partition all would be gathered to the common faith, and one Church formed throughout the whole world.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-98.html]

---

## Verses 5–6

> *Sing praises to the LORD with the lyre, in melodious song with the harp. With trumpets and the blast of the ram’s horn shout for joy before the LORD, the King.*

**Instruments in worship.** The Pulpit Commentary identifies the *chatsotseroth* as the straight silver trumpets used by priests for signals (as on the Arch of Titus), and the *shophar* as the curved ram’s horn. Spurgeon says: “The harps and voices made the sweetness, while the trumpets and horns added the strength; melody and energy should combine in the worship of God.” Gill notes these instruments are described in Old Testament language but that in the New Testament, the saints are said to have “harps in their hands, expressive only of their spiritual melody in their hearts” (Rev 5:8). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-98.html; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps098.php; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-98.html]

**Tradition note — Reformed (Calvin) on instruments:** Calvin took a distinct and influential position: musical instruments belonged to the “puerile instruction of the law” and the temple’s “stated service.” For the Church, “musical instruments in celebrating the praises of God would be no more suitable than the burning of incense, the lighting up of lamps, and the restoration of the other shadows of the law.” He warns against “outward pomp” and says “the simplicity which God recommends to us by the apostle is far more pleasing to him.” Yet he allows that “if believers choose to cheer themselves with musical instruments, they should … make it their object not to dissever their cheerfulness from the praises of God.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-98.html]

**“Before the LORD, the King” (lit. “before the King, the LORD”).** The phrase crowns this section: the joyful noise is directed to Jehovah as King. Spurgeon: “Shall men be more enthusiastic for their earthly princes than for the divine King?” Guzik notes this combination of instruments “assumes some level of effort and skill among the musicians.” [https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps098.php; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-98/]

---

## Verses 7–8

> *Let the sea resound, and all that fills it, the world, and all who dwell in it. Let the rivers clap their hands, let the mountains sing together for joy*

**Creation joins the praise.** The psalm moves from human worshippers using instruments to inanimate creation itself. The sea “roars” (its thunder providing bass), the rivers “clap their hands” (waves dashing against banks like applauding palms), and the hills “sing for joy.” The Pulpit Commentary says the call on nature “is grounded on man’s sympathy with nature, which makes him desire, and half believe, that nature may sympathise with him.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-98.html; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps098.php]

Guzik ties this to Romans 8:19: creation longs for God’s righteous judgment to set all things right. The Expositor’s Bible Commentary notes the bold figure of rivers clapping hands appears also in Isaiah 55:12. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-98/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-98.html]

Spurgeon: “Handel, in some of his sublime choruses, would have been glad of its aid to express his lofty conceptions.” The rivers include “the rolling rivers, the tidal estuaries, the roaring cataracts”; the hills, though silent, are to “burst forth into a sublime uproariousness of mirth.” [https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps098.php]

---

## Verse 9

> *before the LORD, for He comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness and the peoples with equity.*

**The coming Judge as cause for joy.** The reason for creation’s praise is that the Lord comes as Judge. This is not a threat but a promise — His judgment is righteous and equitable. The Pulpit Commentary, quoting Hengstenberg: “God by his righteous judgment will bring the whole earth from a state of sorrow into a state of salvation and joy.” Spurgeon contrasts the first and second advents: “Stiller music … suited his first coming at Bethlehem, but his second advent calls for trumpets, for he is a judge.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-98.html; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps098.php]

**“With righteousness … with equity.”** Guzik notes that in the ancient world, judges were often “bribed or turned by ideology and prejudice”; the prospect of judgment with equity was “a great relief to those who were often oppressed and denied justice.” Kidner, cited by Guzik, says the verse makes the point “which Romans 8:19ff. expounds: that nature will not come into its own until man himself, its proper master, is ruled in righteousness and equity.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-98/]

**Tradition note — Methodist/Wesleyan (Seedbed):** Russell emphasizes that “what makes the Lord’s reign so different from that of other kings or even other gods? It is the Lord’s character. Verse 3 reminded us of God’s love and faithfulness. Verse 9 affirms that God judges with righteousness and fairness. This is a vision our world desperately needs today.” [https://seedbed.com/gods-reign-brings-joy-to-the-world/]

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Emphases Found

| Tradition | Distinctive Emphases |
|---|---|
| **Reformed (Calvin)** | God’s unaided, sovereign arm achieves salvation; musical instruments were ceremonial shadows now fulfilled; the wall between Jew and Gentile is broken down by God alone. |
| **Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill)** | The psalm is a “Coronation Hymn” of the conquering Messiah; Christ’s victory over sin, death, and hell is by moral power not force; the “new song” is tied to the new covenant and Gospel dispensation. |
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik, Enduring Word)** | Emphasises fresh, dynamic worship; the Holy Spirit’s ongoing work; enthusiastic praise involving body and voice; creation eagerly awaiting restoration (Rom 8). |
| **Methodist/Wesleyan (Seedbed)** | Stresses the missional dimension — God’s acts for Israel are for the world; all creation will join in praise; God’s character (love, faithfulness, righteousness) is the foundation for joy. |
| **Anglican/mainstream (Ellicott, Pulpit, Cambridge)** | Psalm belongs to the post-exilic joy of the Restoration; draws heavily on Isaiah 40–66; appointed as an alternative for the *Magnificat* at Evening Prayer. |
